newsitem.title: CHINA: China vows to control Tibet's "splittist" temples.
newsitem.headline: China vows to control Tibet's "splittist" temples.

text.p: China has vowed to bring to heel pro-independence monks and nuns in Tibet with a religious reorganisation campaign to overthrow "splittist" strongholds in the mountain monasteries of the restive Himalayan region.

Three major religious centres had been chosen as test-beds for the campaign to create order and boost patriotic education among Tibet's devout Buddhists, the official Tibet Daily said in its September 7 edition seen in Beijing on Sunday.

"A lot of monasteries have already become bases for splittist activities, and a minority of monks and nuns have become the backbone of the splittists," the newspaper quoted chairman of the Tibet People's Congress, Raidi, as saying.

Officials would focus on establishing political controls in Sera and Drepung monasteries near Lhasa and in the 15th-century mountain-top Ganden monastery to the east of the regional capital, Raidi said in a speech published by the newspaper.
The congress chairman slammed Tibet's supreme spiritual leader the Dalai Lama for tricking monks, nuns and believers into opposing the government and destroying social stability.
"Some temples... are strongholds of the Dalai Lama splittist thinking," Raidi said. "We must resolutely overthrow the strongholds of the Dalai Lama clique."
The main reason for choosing the three large monasteries as test cases was to gain experience with which to direct the reorganisation of monasteries throughout the region, he said.

A London-based Tibet group last month denounced China's attempts to boost patriotic education as ammounting to a purge of dissident monks, with those who refused to sign a pledge of allegiance to China facing expulsion from their monasteries.
Opposition to Beijing rule among Tibetans has led to sporadic riots, underground protests and a spate of bombings in the vast but sparsely populated mountain region.

China had focused on campaigns against independence activists during its "Strike Hard" anti-crime campaign launched in Tibet in April, the Tibet Daily quoted Deputy Secretary Gyaincain Norbu as saying in a speech to senior government officials.
Authorities had cracked more than 30 bombing cases and seized 925 kg (2,039 lb) of explosives, 2008 detonators and 465 metres (1,525 ft) of fuse wire by July 20, Gyaincain Norbu said.
"We must continue to put the war against splittists at the forefront of 'Strike Hard'... the most important cases are those of bombings by splittists," he said.
Leaders and judicial officials should retaliate hard against any riots and disturbances by independence activists while they were still small in scale, he said.

China has this year repeatedly ordered tighter controls in Tibet's monasteries, including the sealing of restive temples and a ban on the display of pictures of the Dalai Lama, Beijing's arch-rival for the loyalties of the Tibetan people.
During a visit to New Zealand last week, the Dalai Lama, who in 1989 won the Nobel Peace Prize for his peaceful campaign for Tibetan autonomy, said time was running out for an agreement with Beijing.
Chinese immigration to Tibet was steadily swamping the native population, he said.
China has ruled Tibet on the basis of historial claim since 1950. The Dalai Lama and thousands of his followers fled into exile in India after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule in 1959.

In a call for action that appeared to suggest mixed loyalties among many of the region's ethnic Tibetan officials, Raidi called for an end to promotions for cadres that secretly supported the Dalai Lama.

"If we promote this kind of official and give them important duties, without a doubt they will become a hidden danger in our Party and government organisations," Raidi said. "They will cause us endless trouble."
